Issued at 116 AM EST Tue Nov 3 2026

             -----------Synoptic Overview-----------

An upper-air disturbance continues to meander in the eastern Gulf
this morning, with vorticity perturbations extending over South
Florida. This feature has become detached from the jet stream and
is expected to weaken further over the next couple of days. It has
interacted with unusually rich moisture and persistent onshore
flow off the Atlantic to produce heavy to extreme precipitation
over parts of the state over the last 48 hours.

The subtropical jet stream remains active across the Central and
Western U.S. A pair of shortwaves is traversing the jet, the first
now reaching Missouri and the second over the Great Basin. These 
two disturbances are forecast to merge into a positively tilted 
trough over the Ohio Valley by Friday. At the surface, high 
pressure should slowly lose its influence over the Eastern 
Seaboard later this week, allowing onshore flow to abate. As the 
trough moves north of Florida from Friday into Saturday, a diffuse
cold front should drift toward the area. The rich moisture 
currently in place will decrease to near or just above seasonal 
norms from late Thursday through at least Saturday. However, the 
late-week cold front brings little to no cold air advection.

By Sunday, ensemble guidance shows a potential phasing of additional
subtropical and polar jet stream energy over the Mississippi Valley,
eventually carving out a trough over the Southeast U.S. by next
Monday. There remains some disagreement in its depth and timing,
but a progressive and positively-tilted trough is favored. Its cold
front is likely to arrive sometime from late Sunday into Monday. A
brief surge of deeper moisture is noted ahead of the front, and
at least modest cold air advection appears likely once it passes.

             -------Sensible Weather & Impacts-------

Now - Tonight...

Following catastrophic flooding across portions of east central
Florida on Monday, even modest additional rainfall could exacerbate
ongoing flooding. Thankfully, the persistent convergence and
forcing responsible for the extreme rainfall have diminished
considerably. However, we still have plentiful moisture and
onshore flow, capable of producing occasional downpours. While
this is expected to produce additional rainfall of less than an
inch in most spots, it won't take much more than that to cause
water levels to rise where flooding is ongoing. The Flood Watch
remains in effect for coastal counties and Okeechobee County
until 10 am, and a Flood Warning continues for areas along the
coast that received the heaviest rainfall totals until 9:30
am. Rain chances today range from 50-60% across much of the area,
but the rain should not be continuous.

Flooding is ongoing in many places, and there are abandoned
vehicles in some neighborhoods. Avoid driving or wading through
floodwater! Flooding will be slow to recede due to saturated 
soils, high water tables, and limited drainage capacity. 

Some breaks of sunshine are expected today, which should warm
many spots back into the lower 80s. Breezy east winds continue,
with gusts 15-25 mph. Rough surf and life-threatening rip currents
persist at all east coast beaches of Central Florida. Additionally,
minor tidal flooding remains possible, especially in Martin County
this afternoon.

Wednesday - Friday...

Onshore flow weakens, but moisture remains sufficient for scattered
showers and isolated storm development on Wednesday. Rain chances
will range from 20% at the coast to 30-50% over the interior. On
average, light rainfall totals are expected. By Thursday and Friday,
deeper moisture will begin to scour out, allowing rain chances to
drop to 20% or less to end the week. Warm temperatures are forecast,
with highs in the mid 80s under partly to mostly sunny skies.

Weekend - Early Next Week...

We should continue our drying trend for much of the weekend, as
rain chances hold at 20% or less. Highs will remain warm in the
lower 80s, but many areas should dip into the 60s at night.

Uncertainty remains, but the next cold front is favored to wait
until Monday to reach Central Florida. The amount of moisture and
the strength of the front will dictate rain chances, which for now
are 20-30%. Some cooler air is expected to follow the front next
week. Statistical guidance currently gives us a 60-70% chance of
failing to reach the 80-degree mark next Tuesday, along with a
50-70% chance of reaching the 50s by next Tuesday night.
